lede: Ask a year group who plays for a sports team and who plays in the orchestra, and some hands go up twice. Counting an 'or' group has the same catch: add the two totals and everybody in both is counted twice. One subtraction puts it right.
can: Work out $P(A \cup B)$ from counts or from given probabilities
Take the overlap off once, so nobody is counted twice
Tell an 'or' question from an 'and' question before you start

md:
A year group of 50 students is asked two questions. 27 play for a sports team, 18 play in the orchestra, and 7 put a hand up for both.
Add 27 and 18 and you get 45. But 12 of the 50 put no hand up at all, so fewer than 45 did at least one: the 7 were counted in each total.

md: Fill a Venn diagram from the overlap outwards. The orchestra total is 18, and 7 of those are in the overlap, so $18 - 7 = 11$ go in the orchestra-only region.

prompt: On the year group's Venn diagram, how many of the 50 students play for a sports team but not in the orchestra? That region is left blank.
explain: $27 - 7 = 20$. The 27 sports players split into the 7 in the overlap and the 20 outside it, just as the orchestra side gave 11.

md:
In everyday speech 'or' can mean one or the other but not both. In probability it never does. $A$ **or** $B$ means at least one of them happens, and that includes the case where both happen.
So the group you want is the whole of both circles together, overlap included, written $A \cup B$ and read 'A union B'.

md: Count the 'or' group region by region and nobody is counted twice: $20 + 7 + 11 = 38$. The two totals give $27 + 18 = 45$ instead.

prompt: In the year group, 27 plus 18 comes to 45, but only 38 students do at least one. Why?
options: The 7 students in both groups are counted in each total
The 12 who do neither were added in by mistake
The two totals should have been multiplied
answer: The 7 students in both groups are counted in each total
explain: Each of those 7 appears once in the 27 and once again in the 18. Take them off once and 38 is left.

text: 2. The rule your formula sheet gives you

md:
Page 2 of the Unit 3 booklet prints $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$.
Add the two probabilities, then subtract the overlap, $P(A \cap B)$, read 'A intersection B'. What is left is the probability of at least one.
Probabilities work the same way. If $P(A) = 0.55$, $P(B) = 0.25$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.1$, then $P(A \cup B)$ is $0.55 + 0.25 - 0.1 = 0.7$.

title: Why subtract once and not twice?
md: Every student in the overlap was counted exactly twice, once in $P(A)$ and once in $P(B)$. Subtracting the overlap once brings each back to a single count; subtract twice and they vanish from the answer.

prompt: For the year group of 50, where 27 play for a sports team, 18 play in the orchestra and 7 do both, work out $P(\text{sports team or orchestra})$. Give a fraction or a decimal.
explain: $\dfrac{27}{50} + \dfrac{18}{50} - \dfrac{7}{50}$ is $\dfrac{38}{50}$, which is 0.76. Leaving the overlap in would give 0.9.

md:
Two events are **mutually exclusive** when they cannot both happen, so $P(A \cap B) = 0$ and the rule loses its last term.
A spinner with 8 equal sections has 3 red, 2 blue and 3 green. One spin cannot land red and blue at once, so $P(\text{red or blue}) = \dfrac{3}{8} + \dfrac{2}{8}$, which is $\dfrac{5}{8}$.

prompt: Which pair of events, for one student in a form group, is mutually exclusive?
options: Born in March, and born in July
Brings a packed lunch, and has a bus pass
answer: Born in March, and born in July
explain: Nobody has two birth months, so that overlap is empty. A student can do both of the other pairs, so each of those needs the subtraction.

text: 4. See it done: a theatre group

md:
A theatre group of 60 members: 31 act, 26 work backstage and 9 do both. One member is chosen at random.
**Step 1.** Name the events, because the rule is written in letters. $A$ is acting, $K$ is backstage.
**Step 2.** Write the three probabilities over the same total: $\dfrac{31}{60}$, $\dfrac{26}{60}$ and $\dfrac{9}{60}$.

**Step 3.** Put them into the rule: $\dfrac{31}{60} + \dfrac{26}{60} - \dfrac{9}{60}$.
The denominators already match, so only the numerators combine. That last line is yours, in the check below.

title: The OR Rule
why: A short run through adding probabilities. It works through mutually exclusive events; the subtraction for events that can both happen is the step this unit adds on top.

prompt: In the theatre group of 60, 31 act, 26 work backstage and 9 do both. What is $P(\text{acts or works backstage})$? Give a fraction or a decimal.
explain: $\dfrac{31 + 26 - 9}{60}$ is $\dfrac{48}{60}$, which is $\dfrac{4}{5}$. The unreduced form earns the same mark.

md:
**Or** means at least one, so you add and take the overlap off once.
**And**, for two events that do not affect each other, means multiply. If the chance of fog tomorrow is $0.2$, the chance of a frost is $0.35$ and the question says the two are independent, then $P(\text{both}) = 0.2 \times 0.35$, which is $0.07$. Fog and frost often come together, so only that sentence lets you multiply.

title: The commonest way this is lost
md: The 2022 report found many candidates adding two probabilities that the question needed multiplied, on one of the easier questions of the paper. Decide 'or' or 'and' in writing before you calculate.

prompt: A bag holds red and blue beads. Which question needs $P(A) \times P(B)$ rather than the addition rule?
options: Two beads are taken, the first put back before the second is drawn. What is the probability that both are red?
One bead is taken. What is the probability that it is red or blue?
One bead is taken. What is the probability that it is not red?
answer: Two beads are taken, the first put back before the second is drawn. What is the probability that both are red?
explain: 'Both' is an 'and' question about two events in turn, and putting the first bead back leaves the second draw unchanged, so the two probabilities multiply. The other two are about one bead and need adding or subtracting.

md:
The rule links four probabilities, so any one of them can be found from the other three. When the union is given, the overlap is $P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cup B)$.
With $P(A) = 0.62$, $P(B) = 0.3$ and $P(A \cup B) = 0.8$, that is $0.62 + 0.3 - 0.8 = 0.12$.

explain: Rearrange the rule: $0.35 + 0.5 - 0.6 = 0.25$. The two probabilities add to more than the union by exactly the overlap.

md: **'During' means at least one.** Summer 2026 asked for rain during a two-day weekend: rain on the Saturday, the Sunday or both, which is an 'or'. With $P(\text{Sat}) = 0.35$, $P(\text{Sun}) = 0.3$ and $P(\text{both}) = 0.1$, it is $0.35 + 0.3 - 0.1 = 0.55$.

**An answer above 1.** Summer 2019 examiners reported probabilities greater than 1: the overlap left in. $0.7 + 0.45 = 1.15$ can never be a probability, so a total like that means the overlap still has to come off.

prompt: The chance of rain on Saturday is $0.45$, on Sunday $0.2$, and on both days $0.05$. What is the probability of rain during the weekend?
explain: 'During the weekend' is at least one of the two days, an 'or': $0.45 + 0.2 - 0.05 = 0.6$.

md:
Read 'or', 'either' and 'during' as at least one, overlap included.
Write the three probabilities over the same total, and subtract the overlap exactly once.
Say when two events are mutually exclusive, so the last term is zero.
Find the overlap from the union by using the rule backwards.
Decide whether a question is an 'or' or an 'and' before you calculate.

In Unit 3 the rule is printed on page 2 and does its work inside the Venn and tree questions, in parts worded with or, either or at least one, usually for two marks. The first mark is the three probabilities written over the same total; the last is the single fraction or decimal. Stuck: draw the two circles, fill the overlap first, and add the regions you need.
